sourceNote: Expanded research-backed senior full-stack interview bank. Question themes were synthesized from current public interview-prep sources covering C#, ASP.NET Core, EF Core, Angular, async/concurrency, SQL, system design, security and performance. Questions are paraphrased and written as original study material; scenario-based interviews remain separate.

questions.question: What is the difference between a class and a struct in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: A class is a reference type; a struct is a value type. I choose based on semantics first: an Order has identity and is normally a class, while a small immutable Money or Coordinate can be a struct.
questions.detailedAnswer: The key differences are copying, identity, nullability, inheritance rules and boxing. Large or mutable structs can be expensive and confusing because assignments copy the value. Structs are strongest for small value-like data.
questions.example: Imagine this concept inside an enterprise ATM or banking application. I would identify where the concept appears in the request or transaction flow, explain the practical problem it solves, and then mention the trade-off I would check before using it in production.
questions.seniorPerspective: A senior answer connects the language rule to domain semantics and performance evidence rather than saying structs are always faster.
questions.commonMistakes: Using a struct only because it is a value type; creating large mutable structs; ignoring boxing and copying.
followUps: Can a struct be null?
What happens when a struct is boxed?
When would readonly struct help?
questions.memoryCue: Remember it as: the difference between a class and a struct in C#.
questions.codeExample:
public class Account { public decimal Balance { get; set; } }
public readonly struct Money { public decimal Amount { get; } public Money(decimal amount) => Amount = amount; }

questions.question: What is the difference between interface and abstract class in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: An interface defines a contract that unrelated types can implement; an abstract class can provide shared state and implementation. I prefer interfaces for replaceable dependencies and abstract classes only when there is real shared behavior.
questions.detailedAnswer: Interfaces support multiple implementations and keep dependencies loosely coupled. Abstract classes are useful when common implementation is part of the design, but they create stronger inheritance coupling.
questions.example: A transaction service can depend on an IPaymentGateway interface. The production implementation talks to the bank, while a test can inject a fake gateway. I would use an abstract class only when several implementations genuinely share workflow and state.
questions.seniorPerspective: The important senior decision is whether the abstraction represents a capability or a shared implementation.
questions.commonMistakes: Creating interfaces for every class without a meaningful boundary; using inheritance just to reuse a few lines of code.
followUps: When would composition be better?
Can a class implement multiple interfaces?
How would you unit test the abstraction?
questions.memoryCue: Remember it as: the difference between interface and abstract class in C#.
questions.codeExample:
public interface IPaymentGateway { Task<bool> PayAsync(decimal amount); }
public abstract class GatewayBase { protected void Log(string message) => Console.WriteLine(message); }

questions.question: What is the difference between IEnumerable and IQueryable?
questions.shortAnswer: IEnumerable represents iteration over data already available to the application, while IQueryable can build an expression that a provider such as EF Core translates into a database query.
questions.detailedAnswer: The boundary is where execution happens. IQueryable is useful at a data-provider boundary; once materialized, subsequent LINQ runs in memory.
questions.example: Imagine this concept inside an enterprise ATM or banking application. I would identify where the concept appears in the request or transaction flow, explain the practical problem it solves, and then mention the trade-off I would check before using it in production.
questions.seniorPerspective: A senior developer watches generated SQL, result size and provider limitations instead of assuming every LINQ expression has the same cost.
questions.commonMistakes: Materializing too early; exposing IQueryable across unrelated layers without control; assuming every C# method can translate to SQL.
followUps: What happens with AsEnumerable?
How do you inspect generated SQL?
When would you intentionally materialize?
questions.memoryCue: Remember it as: the difference between IEnumerable and IQueryable.

questions.question: What are async and await used for in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: They let an application start an asynchronous operation and continue without blocking a thread while I/O is pending. They improve scalability for I/O-bound work; they do not automatically make CPU work faster.
questions.detailedAnswer: Async is most valuable for I/O such as HTTP, database, files and messaging. CPU-heavy work needs a different strategy; wrapping synchronous CPU work in Task.Run inside a server request is not a universal performance fix.
questions.example: If an ATM backend calls a database or another service, the request thread does not need to sit blocked while I/O is running. Using async/await lets the application handle other work while it waits, then continue when the operation completes.
questions.seniorPerspective: I look for end-to-end async flow and avoid blocking with Result or Wait, especially in server code.
questions.commonMistakes: Calling .Result or .Wait; using async void for normal application code; assuming async means parallel.
followUps: Does async create a new thread?
When would Task.WhenAll help?
What happens if one awaited operation fails?
questions.memoryCue: Remember it as: async and await used for in C#.
questions.codeExample:
public async Task<Transaction?> GetAsync(int id)
    => await db.Transactions.FindAsync(id);

questions.question: What are Transient, Scoped and Singleton lifetimes in ASP.NET Core dependency injection?
questions.shortAnswer: Transient creates a new instance each time requested, Scoped normally creates one per request scope, and Singleton keeps one instance for the application lifetime.
questions.detailedAnswer: The lifetime must match state ownership and thread-safety. A singleton must not capture a scoped dependency, and mutable singleton state needs synchronization or should be avoided.
questions.example: An ATM transaction service needs logging, configuration and a database client. Instead of creating each dependency inside the service, the constructor receives them. That makes the service easier to test and lets production configuration decide which implementation is used.
questions.seniorPerspective: I choose a lifetime by ownership and concurrency semantics, not by habit.
questions.commonMistakes: Registering everything as singleton; injecting scoped services into singletons; storing request-specific state in singleton objects.
followUps: What is a captive dependency?
Is DbContext thread-safe?
When would you choose transient?
questions.memoryCue: Remember it as: Transient, Scoped and Singleton lifetimes in ASP.NET Core dependency injection.

questions.question: What is middleware in ASP.NET Core?
questions.shortAnswer: Middleware is a component in the HTTP request pipeline that can inspect, modify, short-circuit or pass a request to the next component.
questions.detailedAnswer: Ordering matters because middleware wraps later components. Authentication must run before authorization, and short-circuiting middleware can prevent the endpoint from executing.
questions.example: For an ATM API, request logging can run early, authentication must run before protected endpoints, and exception handling should be positioned so it can catch downstream failures. Middleware order therefore affects the actual request behavior.
questions.seniorPerspective: I explain middleware as an ordered pipeline and discuss why the order changes behavior.
questions.commonMistakes: Treating middleware order as cosmetic; putting endpoint-specific logic into global middleware; exposing exception details to clients.
followUps: Middleware vs filters?
Where would global exception handling go?
How would you add correlation IDs?
questions.memoryCue: Remember it as: middleware in ASP.NET Core.

questions.question: What is dependency injection and why is it useful?
questions.shortAnswer: Dependency injection supplies a class's dependencies from outside instead of making the class construct them itself. It reduces coupling and improves testing and replacement.
questions.detailedAnswer: Constructor injection makes required dependencies explicit. DI also centralizes lifecycle management and allows infrastructure implementations to change without rewriting business logic.
questions.example: An ATM transaction service needs logging, configuration and a database client. Instead of creating each dependency inside the service, the constructor receives them. That makes the service easier to test and lets production configuration decide which implementation is used.
questions.seniorPerspective: The senior value is not the container itself; it is dependency direction and clear boundaries.
questions.commonMistakes: Injecting dozens of services into one class; hiding required dependencies in service locators; creating infrastructure objects directly inside business logic.
followUps: How do you detect a class with too many dependencies?
When is DI overkill?
How do lifetimes affect DI?
questions.memoryCue: Remember it as: dependency injection and why is it useful.

questions.question: What is the difference between a component and a service in Angular?
questions.shortAnswer: A component owns UI state and presentation behavior; a service encapsulates reusable application logic, data access or shared state.
questions.detailedAnswer: Components should stay focused on the view boundary. Services can be injected and tested independently, but a service should not become a dumping ground for unrelated behavior.
questions.example: In an ATM administration screen, Angular can keep the transaction list in a component and call an API service for data. I would separate presentation from API access, unsubscribe or use appropriate reactive patterns, and avoid unnecessary change detection work on large lists.
questions.seniorPerspective: I use boundaries that make responsibilities and testing obvious.
questions.commonMistakes: Putting all business logic in components; creating a giant shared service; using services as global mutable state without a reason.
followUps: Where should API calls live?
How would components share state?
When would you create a facade?
questions.memoryCue: Remember it as: the difference between a component and a service in Angular.

questions.question: What is the difference between an Observable and a Promise?
questions.shortAnswer: A Promise represents one eventual result, while an Observable represents a stream that can emit values over time and can be composed with RxJS operators.
questions.detailedAnswer: Observables support cancellation and stream composition, which is important for Angular event and HTTP flows. Promises are simpler when only one result matters.
questions.example: In an ATM administration screen, Angular can keep the transaction list in a component and call an API service for data. I would separate presentation from API access, unsubscribe or use appropriate reactive patterns, and avoid unnecessary change detection work on large lists.
questions.seniorPerspective: I choose based on whether the problem is a one-shot result or a stream with composition and cancellation needs.
questions.commonMistakes: Subscribing everywhere without cleanup; nesting subscriptions; using an Observable just because Angular supports it.
followUps: What does switchMap do?
How do you avoid subscription leaks?
When is a Promise simpler?
questions.memoryCue: Remember it as: the difference between an Observable and a Promise.

questions.question: What is Angular change detection?
questions.shortAnswer: Change detection checks whether template-bound values need to be reflected in the DOM. Angular can reduce unnecessary work when components use OnPush and predictable state updates.
questions.detailedAnswer: The important point is not memorizing every internal step; it is controlling state changes and avoiding unnecessary work in large component trees.
questions.example: In an ATM administration screen, Angular can keep the transaction list in a component and call an API service for data. I would separate presentation from API access, unsubscribe or use appropriate reactive patterns, and avoid unnecessary change detection work on large lists.
questions.seniorPerspective: I measure rendering cost before optimizing and keep component state flows explicit.
questions.commonMistakes: Mutating nested objects while expecting OnPush to notice every case; triggering excessive work from template functions; optimizing without profiling.
followUps: What is OnPush?
How do signals interact with change detection?
How would you debug a slow UI?
questions.memoryCue: Remember it as: Angular change detection.

questions.question: What is a closure in JavaScript?
questions.shortAnswer: A closure is a function that retains access to variables from its lexical scope even after the outer function has returned.
questions.detailedAnswer: Closures are useful for encapsulation and callbacks, but long-lived closures can retain references and contribute to memory leaks if attached to long-lived objects or subscriptions.
questions.example: If a UI receives a transaction response asynchronously, I would use promises or async/await for the API call and TypeScript types for the response model. This makes the data flow easier to understand and catches mismatched properties during development.
questions.seniorPerspective: I think about both lexical behavior and object lifetime when using closures.
questions.commonMistakes: Assuming the variables are copied rather than retained by reference; creating accidental long-lived references; confusing closure scope with this binding.
followUps: How does closure differ from this?
Can closures cause memory leaks?
Where have you used closures in UI code?
questions.memoryCue: Remember it as: a closure in JavaScript.

questions.question: What is the difference between let, const and var?
questions.shortAnswer: let and const are block-scoped; var is function-scoped. const prevents reassignment of the binding but does not make an object immutable.
questions.detailedAnswer: Modern TypeScript and JavaScript code normally prefer const by default, let when reassignment is required, and avoid var unless maintaining legacy code.
questions.example: If a UI receives a transaction response asynchronously, I would use promises or async/await for the API call and TypeScript types for the response model. This makes the data flow easier to understand and catches mismatched properties during development.
questions.seniorPerspective: The important interview point is scope and mutation semantics, not simply saying const means immutable.
questions.commonMistakes: Saying const makes objects immutable; using var in new code without a reason; ignoring temporal dead zone behavior.
followUps: What is the temporal dead zone?
Is const object immutable?
How did let fix common loop bugs?
questions.memoryCue: Remember it as: the difference between let, const and var.

questions.question: What is the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN?
questions.shortAnswer: INNER JOIN returns matching rows from both sides. LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table and adds matching right-side data when available.
questions.detailedAnswer: Join choice is driven by the business result set. A LEFT JOIN followed by a WHERE condition on the right table can accidentally behave like an INNER JOIN.
questions.example: If the transaction history screen is slow, I would first inspect the query plan and execution time. If users frequently search by AccountId and TransactionDate, a suitable index can reduce the rows SQL Server needs to scan, but I would verify the write and storage cost too.
questions.seniorPerspective: I verify the expected row cardinality with a small dataset before tuning the query.
questions.commonMistakes: Choosing joins by habit; filtering the right table in WHERE unintentionally; ignoring duplicate rows caused by one-to-many relationships.
followUps: How would you find customers with no orders?
Why can joins multiply rows?
When would EXISTS be better?
questions.memoryCue: Remember it as: the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN.

questions.question: What is an index and why does it improve query performance?
questions.shortAnswer: An index is an additional data structure that helps the database locate rows without scanning the whole table. It speeds some reads but adds storage and write cost.
questions.detailedAnswer: Indexes should follow actual predicates, joins and ordering patterns. Too many indexes increase insert and update cost and can still be ineffective when selectivity is poor.
questions.example: If the transaction history screen is slow, I would first inspect the query plan and execution time. If users frequently search by AccountId and TransactionDate, a suitable index can reduce the rows SQL Server needs to scan, but I would verify the write and storage cost too.
questions.seniorPerspective: I design indexes from query patterns and verify them with execution plans and measured workload.
questions.commonMistakes: Adding an index to every column; ignoring write cost; assuming an index guarantees a seek.
followUps: What is a covering index?
What is a composite index order?
How do you validate an index change?
questions.memoryCue: Remember it as: an index and why does it improve query performance.

questions.question: What is a transaction?
questions.shortAnswer: A transaction groups related database changes so the database can enforce an atomic unit of work according to the chosen isolation level.
questions.detailedAnswer: Transactions protect consistency, but long transactions increase locking and contention. The correct boundary should be as small as possible while protecting the required invariant.
questions.example: If the transaction history screen is slow, I would first inspect the query plan and execution time. If users frequently search by AccountId and TransactionDate, a suitable index can reduce the rows SQL Server needs to scan, but I would verify the write and storage cost too.
questions.seniorPerspective: I define the business invariant first, then choose the smallest transaction that guarantees it.
questions.commonMistakes: Opening transactions around slow external calls; assuming transactions solve distributed consistency; ignoring isolation and lock duration.
followUps: What are ACID properties?
What is isolation level?
How do you handle a transaction failure?
questions.memoryCue: Remember it as: a transaction.

questions.question: What are the main components you consider when designing a backend service?
questions.shortAnswer: I start with clients, API boundaries, business logic, data stores, external dependencies, asynchronous messaging where needed, observability and security.
questions.detailedAnswer: The architecture should follow requirements such as scale, consistency, latency and failure tolerance rather than starting with a list of technologies.
questions.example: For a high-volume transaction service, I would start with the traffic pattern, consistency needs and failure modes. Then I would choose API boundaries, database strategy, caching and asynchronous processing based on those requirements instead of starting with a fashionable architecture.
questions.seniorPerspective: Even a simple design should state assumptions and identify the critical failure paths.
questions.commonMistakes: Jumping directly to Kafka, microservices or Kubernetes; ignoring data ownership; forgetting observability and security.
followUps: How would the design change at 10x traffic?
Where would you cache?
What happens when the database is unavailable?
questions.memoryCue: Remember it as: the main components you consider when designing a backend service.

questions.question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
questions.shortAnswer: Authentication establishes who the caller is; authorization determines what that authenticated identity is allowed to do.
questions.detailedAnswer: Authentication answers identity; authorization answers permission. Authorization must be enforced server-side for protected resources.
questions.example: For an ATM administration API, authentication establishes who the operator is, while authorization checks what that operator is allowed to do. I would enforce authorization on the server rather than relying on the Angular UI to hide buttons.
questions.seniorPerspective: I always separate identity verification from resource-level permission checks.
questions.commonMistakes: Treating a valid JWT as proof that every operation is allowed; relying only on Angular route guards; checking roles without resource ownership where needed.
followUps: What is RBAC?
What is IDOR?
Why can frontend authorization never be the only control?
questions.memoryCue: Remember it as: the difference between authentication and authorization.

questions.question: What is RAG and why is it useful?
questions.shortAnswer: Retrieval-augmented generation retrieves relevant approved information and supplies it to the model before generation, reducing dependence on model memory for changing or private knowledge.
questions.detailedAnswer: A production RAG pipeline needs chunking, metadata, retrieval quality, prompt construction, access control and evaluation; retrieval alone does not guarantee a correct answer.
questions.example: For an AI agent analyzing a production Jira issue, one agent can retrieve the issue, another can inspect logs, and another can compare likely fixes. I would keep tool access controlled, record each step, validate the final result and require human approval before a risky code change is merged.
questions.seniorPerspective: I would measure retrieval and answer quality separately and enforce document-level authorization.
questions.commonMistakes: Using a vector database as a substitute for authorization; retrieving too much context; evaluating only with a few demo questions.
followUps: How do you evaluate retrieval?
How do you prevent cross-tenant retrieval?
What should happen when no relevant document is found?
questions.memoryCue: Remember it as: RAG and why is it useful.

questions.question: What is the difference between Task.WhenAll and awaiting tasks sequentially?
questions.shortAnswer: Task.WhenAll allows independent asynchronous operations to progress concurrently; sequential awaits wait for one operation before starting the next if the tasks are created sequentially.
questions.detailedAnswer: Concurrency is appropriate only when operations are independent and downstream capacity can handle it. It does not make one database query inherently faster.
questions.example: If an ATM backend calls a database or another service, the request thread does not need to sit blocked while I/O is running. Using async/await lets the application handle other work while it waits, then continue when the operation completes.
questions.seniorPerspective: I consider dependency relationships, cancellation, failure handling and downstream load before introducing concurrency.
questions.commonMistakes: Parallelizing dependent operations; firing hundreds of tasks without a limit; forgetting that one failure affects WhenAll completion.
followUps: How are exceptions handled?
How would you limit concurrency?
Can DbContext operations run in parallel?
questions.memoryCue: Remember it as: the difference between Task.WhenAll and awaiting tasks sequentially.

questions.question: What is deferred execution in LINQ and why can it surprise developers?
questions.shortAnswer: Many LINQ operators build a query that executes when enumerated rather than when defined. This means the source can change or expensive work can run multiple times.
questions.detailedAnswer: Materialize deliberately when you need a stable snapshot or when repeated enumeration would be expensive. Keep provider-backed queries controlled so database work is explicit.
questions.example: Suppose I need the successful ATM transactions from the last hour. I can express the filter with LINQ, but with EF Core I also need to check whether the query is translated to SQL efficiently instead of loading thousands of rows into memory first.
questions.seniorPerspective: I watch execution boundaries and do not assume a LINQ variable contains data merely because the query expression was created.
questions.commonMistakes: Calling Count then ToList and accidentally executing two queries; enumerating expensive sequences repeatedly; hiding database calls behind properties.
followUps: When does ToList execute?
What happens with IQueryable?
How would you avoid repeated queries?
questions.memoryCue: Remember it as: deferred execution in LINQ and why can it surprise developers.

questions.question: How does exception handling affect API design?
questions.shortAnswer: Exceptions should represent unexpected or exceptional failures, while expected business outcomes can be modeled explicitly. API middleware should translate unhandled exceptions into consistent responses without leaking internals.
questions.detailedAnswer: A good design separates logging, client response mapping and domain behavior. Exceptions should retain diagnostic context while responses expose only appropriate information.
questions.example: For an ATM transaction API, I would expose clear resources and HTTP semantics, validate requests at the boundary, return meaningful status codes, and make retry-sensitive operations idempotent where possible.
questions.seniorPerspective: I want one consistent error contract, structured logs and clear ownership of where errors are handled.
questions.commonMistakes: Catching Exception everywhere; returning stack traces to clients; logging the same exception at every layer; using exceptions for normal control flow.
followUps: How would you map domain errors to HTTP status codes?
Where should logging happen?
How would you preserve correlation IDs?
questions.memoryCue: Remember it as: exception handling affect API design.

questions.question: How does ASP.NET Core request cancellation work and why should services honor CancellationToken?
questions.shortAnswer: CancellationToken lets a request signal that work is no longer needed. Propagating it to database and HTTP operations can stop wasted work after a client disconnects or a timeout occurs.
questions.detailedAnswer: Cancellation is cooperative. Every layer must accept and pass the token to operations that support cancellation, while cleanup and partial work need explicit consideration.
questions.example: Imagine this concept inside an enterprise ATM or banking application. I would identify where the concept appears in the request or transaction flow, explain the practical problem it solves, and then mention the trade-off I would check before using it in production.
questions.seniorPerspective: I treat cancellation as resource management, not just an API parameter.
questions.commonMistakes: Accepting a token but never passing it onward; swallowing OperationCanceledException incorrectly; assuming cancellation instantly kills every operation.
followUps: Where should the token originate?
How does cancellation affect database calls?
Should cancellation be logged as an error?
questions.memoryCue: Remember it as: ASP.NET Core request cancellation work and why should services honor CancellationToken.

questions.question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization middleware in ASP.NET Core?
questions.shortAnswer: Authentication establishes the ClaimsPrincipal from credentials such as a bearer token. Authorization evaluates policies or roles against that identity and the requested resource.
questions.detailedAnswer: Authentication must occur before authorization. Resource-based authorization can go beyond roles when access depends on ownership or business rules.
questions.example: For an ATM API, request logging can run early, authentication must run before protected endpoints, and exception handling should be positioned so it can catch downstream failures. Middleware order therefore affects the actual request behavior.
questions.seniorPerspective: I design authorization around the protected resource, not only around endpoint roles.
questions.commonMistakes: Assuming authentication means access is granted; putting authorization only in Angular; using roles for every resource rule.
followUps: How do policies work?
What is resource-based authorization?
What response should a forbidden request receive?
questions.memoryCue: Remember it as: the difference between authentication and authorization middleware in ASP.NET Core.

questions.question: How would you prevent an N+1 query problem in EF Core?
questions.shortAnswer: N+1 happens when one query loads a set and then triggers another query for each item. I prevent it with deliberate projection, appropriate eager loading or batched queries.
questions.detailedAnswer: The correct fix depends on the required data shape. Projection can reduce payload and tracking cost; Include is useful when the entity graph itself is needed.
questions.example: In a transaction API, EF Core can load the transaction and related data from SQL. I would keep the DbContext scoped to the request and avoid sharing it across concurrent operations because it represents a unit of work and is not thread-safe.
questions.seniorPerspective: I inspect generated SQL and query counts rather than relying on ORM intuition.
questions.commonMistakes: Adding Include everywhere; lazy loading without awareness; loading full entities when only three fields are needed.
followUps: How would you detect N+1 in production?
When is Include appropriate?
Why is projection often faster?
questions.memoryCue: Remember it as: How would you prevent an N+1 query problem in EF Core.

var orders = await db.Orders
    .Include(o => o.Items)
    .Where(o => o.CustomerId == id)
    .ToListAsync();

questions.question: How does switchMap help with search or autocomplete?
questions.shortAnswer: switchMap switches to the newest inner Observable and unsubscribes from the previous one. It is useful when only the latest user input matters.
questions.detailedAnswer: The operator expresses a business rule: only the latest request matters. For operations that must all complete, mergeMap or another operator may be appropriate.
questions.example: In an ATM administration screen, Angular can keep the transaction list in a component and call an API service for data. I would separate presentation from API access, unsubscribe or use appropriate reactive patterns, and avoid unnecessary change detection work on large lists.
questions.seniorPerspective: I choose an RxJS flattening operator based on concurrency semantics, not by memorizing operator names.
questions.commonMistakes: Using mergeMap for latest-only search; assuming cancellation guarantees the server stops work; nesting subscriptions instead of composing streams.
followUps: switchMap vs concatMap?
What if the request is not cancellable server-side?

questions.question: What is the difference between reactive forms and template-driven forms?
questions.shortAnswer: Reactive forms define form state and validation in TypeScript, while template-driven forms rely more on directives and template configuration. Reactive forms are usually easier to scale and test for complex forms.
questions.detailedAnswer: The choice depends on complexity. Simple forms can be readable with template-driven APIs; large forms benefit from explicit reactive state and validators.
questions.example: In an ATM administration screen, Angular can keep the transaction list in a component and call an API service for data. I would separate presentation from API access, unsubscribe or use appropriate reactive patterns, and avoid unnecessary change detection work on large lists.
questions.seniorPerspective: For enterprise forms I value explicit validation, testability and predictable state transitions.
questions.commonMistakes: Putting complex validation logic into templates; duplicating validation between client and server; forgetting server-side validation.
followUps: How do you implement cross-field validation?
How do you handle dynamic FormArray controls?
Why is server validation still required?
questions.memoryCue: Remember it as: the difference between reactive forms and template-driven forms.

questions.question: What are Angular signals and when would you use them?
questions.shortAnswer: Signals represent reactive state that Angular can track directly. They are useful for local UI state and derived values, while RxJS remains strong for asynchronous streams and event composition.
questions.detailedAnswer: Signals simplify synchronous reactive state. I would not replace every Observable with a signal; the correct abstraction depends on whether the problem is state derivation or asynchronous stream composition.
questions.example: In an ATM administration screen, Angular can keep the transaction list in a component and call an API service for data. I would separate presentation from API access, unsubscribe or use appropriate reactive patterns, and avoid unnecessary change detection work on large lists.
questions.seniorPerspective: I choose signals for clear local reactive state and RxJS where stream operators, cancellation and async composition matter.
questions.commonMistakes: Using effects for ordinary derived state; converting every Observable to a signal without understanding lifecycle; creating hidden side effects.
followUps: Signal vs BehaviorSubject?
What is computed used for?
When would you keep RxJS?

questions.question: How does the JavaScript event loop work?
questions.shortAnswer: JavaScript runs synchronous code on a call stack and uses queues for asynchronous callbacks. Microtasks such as Promise continuations are processed before the next macrotask such as a timer callback.
questions.detailedAnswer: The event loop does not make CPU-heavy JavaScript non-blocking. A long synchronous loop can still freeze the browser even while asynchronous APIs exist.
questions.example: If a UI receives a transaction response asynchronously, I would use promises or async/await for the API call and TypeScript types for the response model. This makes the data flow easier to understand and catches mismatched properties during development.
questions.seniorPerspective: I use the event loop model to reason about ordering, responsiveness and race conditions.
questions.commonMistakes: Saying async code always runs in parallel; ignoring microtask ordering; using setTimeout as a reliable synchronization primitive.
followUps: Promise vs setTimeout ordering?
Why can a browser freeze despite async APIs?
How would you move CPU-heavy work?
questions.memoryCue: Remember it as: the JavaScript event loop work.

questions.question: What is the difference between interface and type in TypeScript?
questions.shortAnswer: Both can describe shapes, but interfaces are designed for object contracts and declaration merging, while type aliases are more flexible for unions, intersections and computed types.
questions.detailedAnswer: The practical difference is expressiveness and API intent rather than a rule that one is always better. Consistency across a codebase matters.
questions.example: If a UI receives a transaction response asynchronously, I would use promises or async/await for the API call and TypeScript types for the response model. This makes the data flow easier to understand and catches mismatched properties during development.
questions.seniorPerspective: I use the construct that best communicates whether I am defining an extensible object contract or a more general type expression.
questions.commonMistakes: Treating interface and type as completely interchangeable; ignoring declaration merging; choosing based only on personal preference in a shared codebase.
followUps: Can interfaces represent unions?
What is declaration merging?
How would you model API success and error results?
questions.memoryCue: Remember it as: the difference between interface and type in TypeScript.

questions.question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
questions.shortAnswer: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
questions.detailedAnswer: Filtering early with WHERE can reduce rows that reach aggregation. HAVING is for conditions on grouped or aggregated results.
questions.example: If the transaction history screen is slow, I would first inspect the query plan and execution time. If users frequently search by AccountId and TransactionDate, a suitable index can reduce the rows SQL Server needs to scan, but I would verify the write and storage cost too.
questions.seniorPerspective: I use the clause that matches the stage of the relational operation and check the execution plan for expensive scans or sorts.
questions.commonMistakes: Using HAVING for ordinary row filters; forgetting grouped columns; assuming SQL evaluates clauses in the textual order they appear.
followUps: Can WHERE use an aggregate?
How would you filter before grouping for performance?
How does GROUP BY affect row count?
questions.memoryCue: Remember it as: the difference between WHERE and HAVING.

SELECT AccountId, SUM(Amount) AS Total
FROM Transactions
WHERE Status = 'Success'
GROUP BY AccountId
HAVING SUM(Amount) > 10000;

questions.shortAnswer: Value types hold their value directly; reference types hold a reference to an object. Assigning a value type copies the value, while assigning a reference type copies the reference.

questions.question: What is a clustered index versus a nonclustered index?
questions.shortAnswer: A clustered index determines the physical/logical organization of table rows around its key in SQL Server, while a nonclustered index is a separate structure that points to the underlying rows.
questions.detailedAnswer: A table has one clustered index at most, while multiple nonclustered indexes can support different access patterns. Indexes improve reads but add write and storage cost.
questions.example: A transaction table might cluster on an appropriate key and add a nonclustered index for frequent searches by terminal ID and transaction time.
questions.seniorPerspective: I design indexes from actual query predicates, joins and ordering, then validate with execution plans and write impact.
questions.commonMistakes: Indexing every column; ignoring key order; assuming an index guarantees a fast query.

questions.question: What is a CTE and when would you use it?
questions.shortAnswer: A common table expression gives a named query expression that can improve readability and support recursive queries. It is not automatically a materialized temporary table.
questions.detailedAnswer: CTEs are useful for breaking complex queries into logical steps, but performance still depends on the resulting execution plan.
questions.example: A reporting query can first define eligible terminals in a CTE and then join transaction totals to that set.
questions.seniorPerspective: I use CTEs to make complex SQL understandable and inspect the plan rather than assuming the CTE itself improves performance.
questions.commonMistakes: Using CTEs as a performance guarantee; building huge nested CTE chains that obscure the query.

questions.question: What is a stored procedure and when would you use one?
questions.shortAnswer: A stored procedure packages database-side logic behind a callable interface. It can be useful for complex database operations, controlled access and established database-centric workflows.
questions.detailedAnswer: Stored procedures are not automatically faster than application code. Their value depends on data locality, operational ownership, security and maintainability.
questions.example: A batch settlement operation that updates several related tables atomically may be a candidate for a stored procedure when database ownership is appropriate.
questions.seniorPerspective: I choose between application logic and database logic based on transaction boundaries, team ownership and operational needs.
questions.commonMistakes: Putting all business logic in stored procedures by default; using dynamic SQL unsafely; making deployment difficult.

questions.question: What is a window function in SQL?
questions.shortAnswer: A window function calculates a value across related rows without collapsing them into one row per group.
questions.detailedAnswer: Functions such as ROW_NUMBER, RANK and SUM OVER are useful for ranking, running totals and latest-record selection.
questions.example: To find the latest transaction per ATM, ROW_NUMBER can partition by terminal and order by transaction time descending.
questions.seniorPerspective: Senior SQL work uses window functions to keep set-based processing in the database instead of procedural loops in application code.
questions.commonMistakes: Using GROUP BY when row-level detail is still needed; misunderstanding partition versus order.

questions.question: What is horizontal scaling versus vertical scaling?
questions.shortAnswer: Vertical scaling gives a machine more resources; horizontal scaling adds more instances. Horizontal scaling can improve capacity and resilience but requires distributed-state considerations.
questions.detailedAnswer: A stateless API is easier to scale horizontally because requests can be routed to different instances.
questions.example: An ATM service can run multiple API instances behind a load balancer while shared state lives in appropriate external systems.
questions.seniorPerspective: I discuss capacity, failure modes, cost and state management rather than treating scaling as simply adding servers.
questions.commonMistakes: Adding instances while a shared in-memory session store becomes the bottleneck; ignoring database capacity.

questions.question: What is a load balancer and why is it used?
questions.shortAnswer: A load balancer distributes requests across healthy service instances and can remove unhealthy instances from rotation.
questions.detailedAnswer: It improves capacity and availability, but session affinity, connection handling, health checks and deployment behavior need consideration.
questions.example: Multiple ATM API instances can sit behind a load balancer so one instance failure does not stop all traffic.
questions.seniorPerspective: I design health checks around actual readiness and distinguish liveness from readiness where appropriate.
questions.commonMistakes: Using a health endpoint that always returns 200; assuming a load balancer fixes every bottleneck.

questions.question: What is a message queue and when would you use one?
questions.shortAnswer: A message queue decouples producers from consumers so work can be processed asynchronously and retried according to defined policies.
questions.detailedAnswer: Queues help absorb bursts and isolate failures, but they introduce delivery semantics, ordering and eventual consistency.
questions.example: After an ATM transaction completes, sending a notification can be queued so a slow SMS provider does not block the transaction API.
questions.seniorPerspective: I define acknowledgement, retry, dead-letter and idempotency behavior before choosing a queue.
questions.commonMistakes: Assuming exactly-once delivery; unlimited retries; putting critical synchronous decisions behind an unbounded queue.
questions.memoryCue: How do you handle poison messages?

questions.question: What is eventual consistency?
questions.shortAnswer: Eventual consistency means different views of distributed data may temporarily disagree but converge after updates propagate.
questions.detailedAnswer: It is a trade-off between immediate consistency and distributed availability/latency. The business operation must tolerate the temporary gap.
questions.example: A transaction dashboard may show a status update a short time after the core transaction system commits it.
questions.seniorPerspective: I identify which data requires strong consistency and which read models can tolerate delay.
questions.commonMistakes: Calling every delayed update a bug; exposing stale data without communicating freshness requirements.

questions.question: What is idempotency and why is it important in distributed systems?
questions.shortAnswer: An idempotent operation can be repeated without producing additional unintended effects. It is important because clients and infrastructure may retry requests.
questions.detailedAnswer: The server can use an idempotency key and persist the result or operation state so a repeated request is recognized.
questions.example: For a cash withdrawal command, a retry must not create a second debit simply because the client did not receive the first response.
questions.seniorPerspective: I design idempotency around a stable business operation key and define how long the key/result is retained.
questions.commonMistakes: Using timestamps as weak identifiers; generating the key only after the operation; making retries safe only for successful cases.
questions.followUps: Where should idempotency keys be stored?

questions.question: How would you design a cache for a read-heavy API?
questions.shortAnswer: I would identify cacheable data, choose a key and TTL, define invalidation behavior, and measure hit rate, staleness and backend load.
questions.detailedAnswer: Caching is a consistency trade-off. Cache stampedes, stale values and memory pressure must be addressed.
questions.example: ATM terminal configuration that changes infrequently can be cached with a controlled TTL and explicit invalidation after updates.
questions.seniorPerspective: I validate cache effectiveness using hit ratio and dependency load rather than assuming every cache improves performance.
questions.commonMistakes: Caching everything; no invalidation plan; unbounded cache growth; caching user-specific data under shared keys.

questions.question: What is SQL injection and how do parameterized queries prevent it?
questions.shortAnswer: SQL injection happens when untrusted input changes the intended SQL command. Parameterized queries send values separately from SQL structure.
questions.detailedAnswer: Input validation is useful, but parameterization is the primary defense for query values. ORMs can help when used correctly.
questions.example: A terminal search value should be passed as a parameter rather than concatenated into a SQL string.
questions.seniorPerspective: I also review dynamic SQL, authorization and database permissions because parameterization does not solve every security issue.

questions.question: What is the principle of least privilege?
questions.shortAnswer: Each identity or service should receive only the permissions required for its job and no more.
questions.detailedAnswer: Least privilege limits blast radius if credentials or components are compromised. It applies to users, APIs, database accounts, service identities and AI tools.
questions.example: An ATM support API may read transaction data but should not have permission to alter database schema.
questions.seniorPerspective: I map permissions to actual operations and review them as responsibilities change.
questions.commonMistakes: Using one powerful database account everywhere; granting admin access for convenience; never reviewing old permissions.

questions.question: What is CORS and what problem does it solve?
questions.shortAnswer: CORS controls which browser origins are allowed to make cross-origin requests to a server. It is a browser security mechanism, not authentication.
questions.detailedAnswer: The server explicitly allows trusted origins and methods. CORS does not stop non-browser clients from calling the API.
questions.example: An Angular application hosted on one trusted domain can call an API on another domain when the API's CORS policy permits that origin.
questions.seniorPerspective: I configure specific origins and credentials behavior instead of allowing every origin in production.
questions.commonMistakes: Using AllowAnyOrigin with credentials; thinking CORS protects the API from Postman or server-side callers.

questions.question: What is CSRF and how is it different from XSS?
questions.shortAnswer: CSRF tricks a browser into sending an unwanted authenticated request; XSS injects executable script into a page or application context.
questions.detailedAnswer: The defenses differ: CSRF protection relies on same-site cookies, anti-forgery tokens and request validation, while XSS defense focuses on output encoding, safe DOM APIs and content security controls.
questions.example: A cookie-authenticated banking portal needs CSRF protection because the browser may automatically attach cookies to forged requests.
questions.seniorPerspective: I first identify the authentication mechanism and browser behavior before selecting the defense.
questions.commonMistakes: Saying CORS alone prevents CSRF; storing untrusted HTML; trusting all client-side validation.

questions.question: What is the difference between latency and throughput?
questions.shortAnswer: Latency is the time for an individual operation; throughput is the amount of work completed per unit time.
questions.detailedAnswer: A system can have good average latency but poor throughput under load, or high throughput with unacceptable response time. Both need measurement.
questions.example: An ATM API might target low transaction latency while also supporting a required number of transactions per second during peak hours.
questions.seniorPerspective: I monitor latency percentiles, throughput, errors and resource saturation together.
questions.commonMistakes: Optimizing only average latency; confusing requests per second with concurrent requests; ignoring saturation.

questions.question: What is a cache stampede and how can you prevent it?
questions.shortAnswer: A cache stampede happens when many requests miss the same expired value and all hit the backend simultaneously.
questions.detailedAnswer: Mitigations include request coalescing, jittered TTLs, background refresh and stale-while-revalidate depending on correctness needs.
questions.example: If terminal configuration expires from cache during a traffic spike, hundreds of requests should not all query the database at once.
questions.seniorPerspective: I choose the mitigation based on backend capacity and data freshness requirements and monitor cache-miss bursts.
questions.commonMistakes: Adding a cache without considering synchronized expiry; refreshing everything at once; serving stale data without an explicit policy.

questions.question: What is RAG and how is it different from fine-tuning?
questions.shortAnswer: RAG retrieves relevant external information at query time and gives it to the model as context. Fine-tuning changes model behavior through additional training data.
questions.detailedAnswer: RAG is useful when knowledge changes frequently or must be grounded in private documents. Fine-tuning is better suited to behavior, style or task adaptation rather than simply storing current facts.
questions.example: A production-support assistant can retrieve Jira issues, logs and approved documentation before generating a diagnosis.
questions.seniorPerspective: I separate retrieval quality, generation quality and authorization because a strong model cannot compensate for missing or unauthorized context.
questions.commonMistakes: Treating RAG as a guarantee against hallucination; indexing sensitive data without access controls; fine-tuning just to add changing facts.

questions.question: How would you evaluate an enterprise AI assistant?
questions.shortAnswer: I would evaluate retrieval relevance, groundedness, answer correctness, refusal behavior, latency, cost and security using a representative test set.
questions.detailedAnswer: A production evaluation should include both successful questions and adversarial or unanswerable questions. Human review remains useful for ambiguous quality dimensions.
questions.example: For a Jira troubleshooting assistant, I would build a benchmark of real issue types and measure whether cited evidence actually supports the proposed diagnosis.
questions.seniorPerspective: Senior AI engineering treats evaluation as a regression system that runs whenever prompts, models, retrieval or tools change.
questions.commonMistakes: Measuring only user thumbs-up; testing only easy questions; ignoring access-control failures and cost.
